summary: Extends OSPF versions 2 and 3 to flood traffic engineering information about links between Autonomous Systems, supporting MPLS and GMPLS TE path computation across multiple ASes. It does not define flooding of information from one AS into another. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Routers tell their neighbors about the roads they can use. This lets them also share facts about the bridges that lead out to other networks, so trip planners can use them.

questions: ospf extensions for inter-as traffic engineering
how does ospf flood inter-as te links
what is the remote as number sub-tlv
how does ospf advertise inter-as te links
subtitle: New OSPF advertisements that let routers learn about the TE links leading from their network into a neighboring one.

tldr.problem: To compute an MPLS or GMPLS traffic engineering path across several Autonomous Systems, a path computation entity must know which links connect to other ASes, their TE properties, the neighbor's AS number and the neighboring ASBR.
tldr.mechanism: OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 get two new LSA types (Inter-AS-TE-v2 and Inter-AS-TE-v3) and three new sub-TLVs in the Link TLV that name the remote AS and remote ASBR. The ASBR advertises its own side of the link and, as a proxy, the neighbor's side.
tldr.outcome: Path computation can pick the right exit ASBR using inter-AS link information, while nothing is flooded from one AS into another and no OSPF adjacency forms on the inter-AS link.

today: RFC 5392 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
OSPF-TE (RFC 3630) lets OSPF flood traffic engineering (TE) information about links inside an area, using Type 10 Opaque LSAs. RFC 5329 does the same for OSPFv3. A Link TLV carries nested sub-TLVs that describe the attributes of one TE link.

To set up MPLS-TE label switched paths across multiple Autonomous Systems (ASes), a path computation entity needs TE information about links that connect to other ASes. That entity may be the head-end LSR, an AS Border Router (ASBR) or a Path Computation Element (PCE). RFC 5392 defines two new LSAs, one for OSPFv2 and one for OSPFv3, and three new sub-TLVs in the Link TLV.
sections.eli5: Inside one network, routers already know the roads. To plan a trip that crosses several networks, the planner also needs to know about the border crossings.

sections.title: The Problem: Choosing an Exit Across ASes
sections.content:
The RFC describes two ways of finding an inter-AS path. In the per-domain method, an entry router that receives a Path message whose ERO names the next AS must work out which ASBRs in its own AS connect to that AS, and whether their TE connectivity (such as available bandwidth) is adequate.

In backward recursive path computation (BRPC), PCEs in each AS cooperate along a chain. A PCE must know which boundary ASBRs connect to the upstream AS and the TE properties of those links.

Both cases need the same facts: the list of inter-AS TE links of the local AS, the TE properties of each link, the AS number of the neighbor it reaches, and the TE Router ID of the neighboring ASBR. This information may be needed throughout the AS if path computation is fully distributed.
sections.eli5: Picture choosing which gate to leave a city by. You need to know which gates lead to the next city you want, and how crowded each one is.

sections.title: What Is Deliberately Left Out
sections.content:
The RFC lists explicit non-objectives. It makes no attempt to distribute TE information from within one AS to another, and no mechanism to distribute TE reachability for destinations outside the AS. It proposes no change to the PCE architecture, does not support or recommend TE aggregation, involves no exchange of private information between ASes, and forms no OSPF adjacencies on the inter-AS link.

It also notes that it does not overlap with L1VPN auto-discovery (RFC 5252), which deals with CE-PE links.
sections.eli5: Each network keeps its own secrets. Only the facts about the border gates are shared inside a network, and nothing is passed across the border.

sections.title: The Two New LSAs
sections.content:
For OSPFv2, the Inter-AS-TE-v2 LSA is a new Opaque LSA with the same format as the Traffic Engineering LSA of RFC 3630. Its Opaque type is 6. It SHOULD be carried in a Type 10 (area-scoped) Opaque LSA, or MAY be carried in a Type 11 (AS-scoped) one when the information should reach all routers in the AS. This is an AS-wide policy choice, and ASBR implementations SHOULD provide configuration control of it.

For OSPFv3, the Inter-AS-TE-v3 LSA uses a new LS type function code, 13. The U-bit is always set to 1, so routers flood it even if they do not recognize the type. The S2 and S1 bits SHOULD be 01 (area scope) but MAY be 10 (AS scope), again as a network-wide policy choice.

Both LSAs contain one top-level TLV, the Link TLV (type 2).
sections.eli5: There are two new kinds of notice, one for each OSPF version. Each can be posted just in one neighborhood or all across the network, whichever the network owner decides.

sections.title: The New Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Link ID sub-TLV MUST NOT be used in an Inter-AS-TE-v2 LSA, and the Neighbor ID sub-TLV MUST NOT be used in an Inter-AS-TE-v3 LSA, because OSPF is an IGP and these are not applicable to inter-AS links. Instead the remote ASBR is identified with three new sub-TLVs.

  • Remote AS Number (type 21, four octets): the neighboring AS. It MUST be included. When only two octets are used for the AS number, the high-order two octets MUST be zero.
  • IPv4 Remote ASBR ID (type 22, four octets): any stable, routable IPv4 address of the remote ASBR. Using its TE Router ID is RECOMMENDED.
  • IPv6 Remote ASBR ID (sixteen octets): a stable, routable, global IPv6 address of the remote ASBR, with its IPv6 TE Router ID RECOMMENDED. The IANA section assigns type 24, while the list in section 3.2.1 of the RFC says 23.

At least one of the two ASBR ID sub-TLVs SHOULD be present. In OSPFv2 the IPv4 one MUST be included if the neighbor has an IPv4 address, otherwise the IPv6 one MUST be used, and OSPFv3 mirrors this. Both MAY be present, and either kind may appear in either LSA, since they refer to a different AS.
sections.eli5: Each border notice says which network is on the other side and gives the ID of the router there, like writing the neighbor's street name and house number.

sections.title: How an ASBR Advertises the Link
sections.content:
When TE is enabled on an inter-AS link and the link is up, the ASBR SHOULD advertise it with the normal OSPF-TE procedures. It SHOULD withdraw the advertisement when the link goes down or TE is disabled, and re-advertise on parameter changes, while taking precautions against excessive re-advertisements. Hellos MUST NOT be exchanged over the link, so no OSPF adjacency is formed.

Normally both ends of a TE link emit LSAs, so the database holds both directions and CSPF can do a two-way check. With no IGP peering across ASes, the ASBR instead acts as a proxy: it advertises its own side and an additional LSA describing the other ASBR's view. Only essential information (Link Type, Remote AS number, Remote ASBR ID) must be advertised. Legacy routers ignore these advertisements because the Link Type is an unknown value, but they keep flooding the LSA.

Path computation entities SHOULD NOT use these links to exit an AS and immediately re-enter it through another TE link, except under specific policy. The data comes from configuration at the ASBR, and some may be obtainable from BGP; how is an implementation matter.
sections.eli5: Since the other network will not talk to this one directly, the border router writes both sides of the notice itself, using what it was told about its neighbor.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions are relatively minor and can be secured inside the AS by existing OSPF security mechanisms. There is no exchange of information between ASes, so no OSPF security is required between them.

The remote AS number and remote ASBR ID are often obtained manually from a neighboring administration as part of a commercial relationship, so their source and content should be carefully checked before entry. If a BGP peering exists between the two ASBRs, a remote AS number in a BGP OPEN that differs from the one configured for OSPF-TE can reveal a mistake. Local policy SHOULD then decide whether to alert the operator or suppress the advertisement.
sections.eli5: The neighbor's details are typed in by a person, so double-check them. If the two border routers already talk another way, they can compare notes and catch mistakes.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned Opaque LSA type 6 to the Inter-AS-TE-v2 LSA and OSPFv3 LSA function code 13 to the Inter-AS-TE-v3 LSA. In the sub-registry "Types for sub-TLVs in a TE Link TLV", it assigned 21 (Remote AS Number), 22 (IPv4 Remote ASBR ID) and 24 (IPv6 Remote ASBR ID).
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers got three new entries for the new kinds of notes, plus one number for each new notice type.
